title: Pavlo Tychyna

fields.label: Position held
fields.value: Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada, deputy of the Supreme Soviet of the Soviet Union

summary: Pavlo Hryhorovych Tychyna was a prominent Ukrainian poet, translator, publicist, and statesman, born on January 23, 1891, in Pisky, Ukraine. He is best known for composing the lyrics of the Anthem of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic and for his complex relationship with the Soviet regime.

sections.heading: Early Life
paragraphs: Pavlo Tychyna was born in Pisky, [[ukraine|Ukraine]], in 1891 and was baptized on January 27, a date that was mistakenly regarded as his birth date until recently. His father, Hryhoriy Timofiyovych Tychynin, served as a village deacon and teacher, while his mother, Maria Vasylivna Tychynina, was eleven years younger than him. He grew up in a large family with nine siblings, consisting of five sisters and four brothers. Tychyna began his education at the local elementary school, which opened in 1897, and was influenced by his first teacher, Serafima Morachevska, who encouraged him to join a choir. By 1900, he was a member of an archiary chorus at the Trinity monastery near [[chernihiv|Chernihiv]] and attended the Chernihiv theological school. After his father's death in 1906, he completed his schooling in 1907.

From 1907 to 1913, Tychyna studied at the Chernihiv Theological Seminary, where he befriended future poet Vasyl Ellan-Blakytny and met writer Mykhailo Kotsiubynsky, who impacted his early literary development. His works began appearing in local publications from 1912 to 1913. He later attended the Economics department of the [[kyiv|Kyiv]] Commercial Institute from 1913 to 1917, although he did not graduate. During this time, he was involved with the editorial boards of the Kyiv newspaper [[verkhovna-rada|Rada]] and the magazine Svitlo and worked at the Chernihiv statistical bureau.

sections.heading: Literary Career and Political Involvement
paragraphs: Tychyna's literary career gained momentum during World War I when he worked with various [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] publications. In 1920, he published 'Pluh' and subsequently moved to [[kharkiv|Kharkiv]] in 1923, engaging with early post-Revolution Ukrainian literary organizations. He became a member of the literary organization Hart and later joined VAPLITE in 1927. In the 1920s, he also served on the Kharkiv City Council as an independent politician. However, ideological controversies surrounding VAPLITE and Tychyna's poetry led to criticism, prompting him to cease writing temporarily.

Despite the challenges, he later became a member of Chervonyi Shliakh and pursued studies in Armenian, Georgian, and Turkic languages while actively participating in the Association of Eastern Studies in Kyiv.

sections.heading: Submission to Soviet Authority
paragraphs: In the early 1930s, Tychyna aligned himself with the socialist-realist ideology endorsed by the Communist Party, which has been interpreted as a capitulation to the Soviet regime. He held the position of head of the Institute of Literature of the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences from 1936 to 1939 and again from 1941 to 1943. He was also a deputy of the Supreme Soviet of the [[ukrainian-soviet-socialist-republic|Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic]] starting in 1938. In 1941, he received the [[donetsk|Stalin]] Prize for literature for his works that praised Joseph Stalin.

The Second World War influenced Tychyna's poetry, leading him to produce several patriotic poems. He served as the Minister of Education of the Ukrainian SSR from 1943 to 1948 and became a deputy of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR in 1946. Tychyna chaired the Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian SSR from 1953 to 1959, but he did not participate in the Ukrainian cultural revival in the postwar period.

sections.heading: Later Life and Legacy
paragraphs: In his final decade, Tychyna continued to write poetry that celebrated the Communist Party, focusing on themes related to collective farms and Soviet leaders. His work became increasingly viewed as outdated and self-parodic during the era of Leonid Brezhnev, although some of his earlier talent was still evident in his postwar poems. Tychyna was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1967 by Omeljan Pritsak, but he passed away in September of that year. His collaboration with Soviet authorities led to a forced retraction of his Nobel candidacy, likely due to his Ukrainian background.

Tychyna's literary contributions include notable works such as 'Clarinets of the Sun' (1918), 'The Plow' (1919), and 'The Party is our Guide' (1934). His poetry has been translated into English, and he received several awards, including the Stalin Prize and the Shevchenko National Prize in 1962.

sections.heading: Cultural Impact and Commemoration
paragraphs: Pavlo Tychyna's legacy is commemorated in various ways across Ukraine, with streets named after him in cities such as Kyiv, Chernihiv, and [[lviv|Lviv]]. Memorial plaques can be found in Kyiv, Chernihiv, and Kharkiv, while a museum dedicated to his life and work exists in Kyiv. His poetry has also inspired modern pop songs, reflecting his enduring influence on Ukrainian culture.
